PLOS Computational Biology.title: Statistical analysis of residue contact energies reveals folding determinants of ion channels
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Svetlana I. Tarnovskaya, Boris S. Zhorov, Denis B. Tikhonov Tetrameric and pseudo-tetrameric cationic channels, which are targeted by many drugs and toxins, play key roles in the cell physiology and pathophysiology. This diverse superfamily of P-loop channels includes but is not limited to voltage-gated potassium, sodium and calcium channels, TRP channels, and ionotropic glutamate receptors. In hundreds of crystal and cryoEM structures of P-loop channels, the general folding is rather similar but subfamily-specific structural details vary greatly. The latter underlie atomic mechanisms of ion selectivity, gating, sensitivity to drugs and toxins, and dysfunction of thousands disease-associated variants. Understanding these mechanisms may benefit from comparative analyses of multiple structures. Here, we propose a statistical method to reveal structural determinants of folding in related proteins, which involves clustering of residue-residue contact energies. We applied the method to a pH-gated potassium channel KcsA and a voltage-gated sodium channel NavAb. Twenty 3D-aligned experimental structures of each channel with universal residue labels were downloaded from database www.plic3da.com and Monte Carlo energy minimized. Residue contact energies clustered in the multidimensional space of contacts automatically discriminated open vs. closed states of KcsA, and wild-type vs. chimeric structures of NavAb. We found and analyzed specific contacts that underlie structural peculiarities. The proposed approach may help detecting folding peculiarities and their structural determinants between subfamilies of P-loop channels, within individual subfamilies, and could be adapted to other proteins.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Multi-model forecasting of respiratory disease activity in Germany during the 2024–2025 season
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Johannes Bracher, Daniel Wolffram, Rodrigo Amaral Lind, Nils Bardeck, Micha Böhm, Seba Contreras, Philipp Dönges, Felix Günther, Rolf Kaiser, Jan van de Kassteele, Alexander Kuhlmann, Berit Lange, Barbora Němcová, Viola Priesemann, Ulrich Reinacher, Isti Rodiah, Frank Sandmann, the RESPINOW Study Group , Melanie Schienle Respiratory diseases cause considerable morbidity in autumn and winter and are a priority in public health monitoring. In Germany, they are subject to a number of surveillance systems, including both pathogen-specific and syndromic indicators. In this paper we present a collaborative multi-target and multi-model real-time forecasting system rolled out during the 2024/25 season, and discuss differences to earlier efforts carried out during the COVID-19 pandemic. We focus on general practitioner consultations for acute respiratory infections (ARI) and hospitalizations for severe acute respiratory infections (SARI), where a total of eight models were run to generate nowcasts and forecasts. In addition, we consider confirmed cases of seasonal influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) where one forecasting model each was available. As all indicators were subject to retrospective revisions, forecasting models were combined with a nowcasting step. For the SARI and ARI indicators, we combined the available models into an ensemble and conducted detailed quantitative evaluations. Nowcasts overall showed convincing performance, even though for some models Christmas break effects led to an upward bias in early January. Forecasts were overall well-calibrated and most models outperformed simple benchmark models. When taking into account age-stratified targets, most observed performance differences to a persistence baseline were statistically significant. Anticipating the peak timing and magnitude, however, proved to be challenging, with many models predicting too flat curves with a too early turnaround (e.g., in late January rather than mid-February for SARI). The combined ensemble forecast was among the best-performing approaches, but unlike in previous related projects did not consistently outperform individual models. We conclude by discussing learnings on the organization of collaborative forecasting projects in post-COVID-19 times.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: AlphaFold models of host-pathogen interactions elucidate the prevalence and structural modes of molecular mimicry
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Delora Baptista, Lidia Gomez-Lucas, Jürgen Jänes, Nevan J. Krogan, Maria João Amorim, Ylva Ivarsson, Pedro Beltrao Pathogens exploit host cellular machinery through protein-protein interactions (PPIs), often using molecular mimicry to hijack host cellular processes. While there have been thousands of host-pathogen PPIs determined to date, the lack of structural information for these impedes the study of the prevalence of molecular mimicry and convergent evolution of protein interaction interfaces. To address this, we benchmarked AlphaFold2 and 3 for prediction of structures of host-pathogen interactions observing that accurate models can be retrieved when ranking by modelling confidence, despite an overall low performance. We predicted structures for 6,782 pathogen-human PPIs yielding 803 models of higher confidence. Most pathogen proteins interacting with a common human protein are predicted to do so via the same interface, suggesting a high degree of convergent evolution of protein interaction interfaces. When comparing structural models from host-pathogen and host-host interactions, we observe that a majority of pathogen proteins are predicted to target existing human PPI interfaces. We categorized instances of mimicry into different modes, occurring at different frequencies: 1) via the same domain family (least common); 2) via a similar structural motif; and 3) via a similar linear peptide (most common). We selected examples of linear peptide interactions for binding assay testing, confirming 8 out of 12 predicted interfaces, including 3 viral linear peptide interactions. This validates AlphaFold’s ability to model some host-pathogen interactions and the mechanisms underlying molecular mimicry. This work showcases the value of large-scale structural modelling to study convergent evolution of host-pathogen interactions and how molecular mimicry may contribute to infection or host defense.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Large-scale analysis of AlphaFold structures reveals organism-specific physicochemical signatures
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Michael J. Stam, Diego A. Oyarzún, Nadanai Laohakunakorn, Christopher W. Wood Recent advancements in protein structure prediction methods have ushered in a new era of abundant and accurate structural data, providing opportunities to analyse proteins at a scale that has not been possible before. Here we performed a large-scale analysis of physicochemical properties across 373,779 confident AlphaFold structures. Our analysis revealed systematic variation between proteins from different organisms to such an extent that major features of the tree of life could be recovered from these data. Surprisingly, this relationship persisted even when we restricted our analysis to eukaryotic, cytosolic proteins and proteins from single AlphaFold Database Foldseek clusters. Given the strong functional constraints on protein chemistry, this finding is unexpected and suggests that protein structures have organism-specific physicochemical signatures, which might reveal evolutionary constraints imposed by the cellular environment and could have significant implications for the design and engineering of novel proteins.

Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution.title: Phylogenomic analyses shed new light on the phylogeny and historical biogeography of the water lily genus Nymphaea (Nymphaeaceae).
Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution.abstract: Nymphaea is the most species-rich, geographically widespread, and phenotypically diverse genus in the basal angiosperm order Nymphaeales. Species of this genus possess considerable ornamental, cultural, medicinal, and ecological value. However, phylogenetic relationships among species and the biogeographic history of this genus remain incompletely understood. Here, we conducted a comprehensive phylogenomic study of Nymphaea using cytoplasmic (plastid and mitochondrial) and nuclear genomic sequence data. Our phylogenetic analyses supported the merger of the genera Victoria and Euryale into Nymphaea. The significant phylogenetic discordance detected within Nymphaea was attributed to both incomplete lineage sorting and reticulate evolution. Moreover, network analyses suggested that hybridization and "ghost introgression" have likely been widespread throughout the evolutionary history of the genus. Molecular dating and biogeographic analyses indicated that Nymphaea originated in the Oriental region during the mid-Cretaceous and subsequently dispersed to other regions, where multiple centers of diversification were established. Long-distance dispersal and vicariance appear to have jointly shaped the intercontinental distribution of the genus. These findings provide new insights into the phylogeny and evolutionary history of Nymphaea.

mSphere.title: "What's SUPP": developing an in vitro model for healthy oral biofilms.
mSphere.abstract: Oral diseases such as caries and periodontitis coincide with dysbiosis of oral plaque biofilms enriched for oral pathogens typically present in low abundance in health. Many available in vitro supragingival plaque (SUPP) models favor the growth of oral pathogens via several factors, including anaerobic incubation, non-saliva media, or assembled consortia that do not well represent species abundant in healthy SUPP. Here we present a low-cost, high-throughput in vitro SUPP model designed to study healthy commensal interactions. Saliva-coated hydroxyapatite discs, inoculated with donor SUPP, were incubated aerobically under a thin layer of medium. In this context, we performed an iterative 16S rRNA microbiome profiling-guided refinement of medium and incubation conditions to best match donor SUPP composition. Using a 25% saliva medium, we obtained in vitro SUPP community diversity over 3-5 days that more closely resembled in vivo diversity than those using rich media or anaerobic incubation. Using these initial model conditions, we were able to determine how filter vs boiling sterilization of saliva impacted community composition in vitro. Furthermore, we were able to use the model to quantify the fitness of the fluorescently labeled Corynebacterium matruchotii wild-type and lut-operon mutant, demonstrating their integration into the in vitro SUPP biofilm and the necessity of lut expression in vitro in a far more complex community than we had previously investigated. This model enables a low-cost mechanistic investigation of polymicrobial interactions in a structurally complex, health-relevant biofilm context at suitable sample sizes for microbiome assessment independent of host immune responses.IMPORTANCEMultiple oral diseases coincide with a shift in the oral microbiota that occurs during a complex transition, which can also be impacted by changes in the host environment and immune response. We currently know relatively little of interactions and mechanistic relationships within polymicrobial communities in oral health compared to disease. While the focus on disease research is rightfully justified, the understanding of what mechanisms might serve to stabilize or restore healthy communities may be a promising avenue for disease prevention and treatment. The significance of this study is that it provides an initial, accessible in vitro model to study these mechanisms of interaction separate from host responses. Use of this model will enable discovery of microbial-driven factors that may preserve or restore oral health.

Journal of Evolutionary Biology.title: Sexual dimorphism in weapons arises from amplification of shared developmental pathways.
Journal of Evolutionary Biology.abstract: Sexually selected traits are expected to be especially sensitive to developmental condition, but the pathways generating sex differences in environmental sensitivity remain unclear. We manipulated juvenile nutrition and developmental group size in European earwigs (Forficula auricularia sensu lato) and fitted a combined-sex Bayesian structural equation model linking development time, body size, forceps length, and elytra length. Compared with the standard diet, the nutrient-diluted diet reduced forceps length in both sexes, with a substantially greater reduction in males through both direct and growth-mediated pathways. Rearing with 4 or 8 nymphs rather than 1 nymph also increased male forceps more strongly, primarily through direct, body-size-independent paths. These sex differences were much larger for forceps than for elytra, a nonweapon comparison trait. The pronotum-forceps relationship was markedly stronger in males, whereas treatment effects on pronotum length were broadly similar between sexes. Development time and forceps length were negatively correlated among maternal families in males; the corresponding female association was similar in direction but less precise. The same hypothesised developmental cascade was therefore consistent with both sexes, but male weapon expression showed stronger environmental responsiveness and greater amplification of body-size variation.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Molecular assay development and validation using ITS1 and HSP70 gene targets for identifying Leishmania species in American cutaneous leishmaniasis in the State of Amazonas, Brazil.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Leishmaniasis, caused by protozoa of the genus Leishmania, presents diverse clinical forms. In Brazil, L. (Viannia) braziliensis and L. (V.) guyanensis are the main species causing cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL). Species identification is essential, as treatment differs. Antimonial meglumine or amphotericin B is recommended for L. (V.) braziliensis, while pentamidine or amphotericin B for L. (V.) guyanensis. Conventional diagnostic methods often lack sensitivity and ability to identify the parasite species for tailoring proper treatment. Molecular identification provides a sensitive alternative for accurate diagnosis, epidemiological assessment, and treatment guidance. This study developed and validated a molecular assay targeting the ITS1 and HSP70 genes to detect and identify Leishmania species in clinical samples. Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) assays with TaqMan probes targeting the ITS1 and HSP70 genes were developed to detect Leishmania subgenera and species in biopsy and filter paper samples. Diagnostic accuracy and test agreement were assessed. The assays demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy. ITS1 revealed 99.7% sensitivity and 94% specificity, and HSP70 showed 99.6% sensitivity and 95% specificity compared with microscopy detection. Agreement with direct microscopy was high (Kappa = 0.95-0.96). Species identification revealed L. (V.) guyanensis (83%), L. (V.) braziliensis (12%), L. (Leishmania) amazonensis (3%), L. (V.) lainsoni (1.7%), and L. (V.) naiffi (0.3%). The qPCR panel represents a significant advance in molecular diagnosis of leishmaniasis, combining high sensitivity, specificity, and practical applicability. It provides accurate species identification and offers essential support for effective epidemiological surveillance and target therapy in endemic regions. [IMPORTANCE] American cutaneous leishmaniasis diagnosis in endemic regions, such as the State of Amazonas (Brazil), remains challenging, as conventional methods often fail to detect low parasite infections or identify species. This study addresses this diagnostic gap by developing and validating a dual-target quantitative polymerase chain reaction panel with the ITS1 and HSP70 genes. This assay demonstrated excellent diagnostic accuracy (AUC > 0.95). The high sensitivity and compatibility with filter paper samples provide a less invasive and more practical solution for sample collection and transport. Implementation of this molecular tool is fundamental to facilitating epidemiological surveillance and ensuring species-specific treatment for the parasite.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Genetic variability of the pneumococcal wciZ-gene and how it relates to capsule-type prediction.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Streptococcus pneumoniae serotypes 15B and 15C differ solely in the O-acetylation state of their capsular polysaccharides, determined by the activity of the wciZ-encoded O-acetyltransferase. Variation in the number of thymine-adenine (TA) repeats within the wciZ reading frame can induce frameshift events, resulting in either functional (15B) or non-functional (15C) enzyme variants. To characterize wciZ diversity and assess the accuracy of genome-based capsule-type prediction models, the wciZ TA repeat regions of all serotype 15B and 15C isolates from Germany's national invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) surveillance 2022-2024 were analyzed. A total of 364 wciZ genes were partially sequenced, revealing 19 distinct TA repeat variants. In addition to known repeat counts, previously unreported variants with 2, 12, 13, 14, and 15 repeats were identified. Two novel mutational mechanisms influencing serotype expression emerged: (i) a single thymine deletion upstream of the repeat region, potentially abolishing enzyme activity even when the reading frame is restored, and (ii) a 13-nucleotide deletion downstream of the repeats, causing premature translational termination despite eight TA repeats normally associated with serotype 15B. The distribution of repeat numbers showed a steep, right-skewed, unimodal profile with eight repeats predominating, suggesting a mutational hotspot, and a three-repeat expansion consistently resulting in a 15B phenotype. The SeroBA version currently implemented in the PathogenWatch pipeline correctly predicted most identified variants; however, rare mutations outside the TA repeat region, particularly mutations restoring the reading frame while potentially impairing enzyme function, can compromise prediction accuracy and should be considered in future genome-based serotyping frameworks. [IMPORTANCE] Streptococcus pneumoniae is a major cause of invasive infections, including pneumonia, sepsis, and meningitis. This makes the accurate surveillance and characterization of circulating strains essential for the development of effective prevention strategies. Among pneumococci, serotypes 15B and 15C are a notable example of how subtle genetic changes can result in different capsule phenotypes, which can have significant diagnostic and epidemiological implications. This study reveals that the molecular basis of the 15B/15C switch is more complex than previously assumed, demonstrating unexpected genetic diversity and novel mutational mechanisms within the wciZ gene that distinguish the serotypes. The study demonstrates that serotype assignment based solely on thymine-adenine repeat counts can result in systematic misclassification. By improving our understanding of capsule variation between serotypes 15B and 15C, this study provides valuable insights into genome-based serotyping, enhances the interpretation of surveillance data, and emphasizes the necessity of continuously reassessing molecular prediction.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Blood transcriptional signatures reflect pulmonary inflammatory programs in Mycobacterium tuberculosis-infected C3HeB/FeJ mice.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Blood transcriptional signatures have been widely investigated as biomarkers for distinguishing tuberculosis (TB) disease states in humans. Previous studies have also shown that the peripheral blood transcriptional profiles of Mycobacterium tuberculosis-infected C3HeB/FeJ mice recapitulate key features of human active TB blood signatures. However, the extent to which these peripheral blood responses reflect localized transcriptional programs in infected lungs remains unclear. In this study, we performed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) in parallel on lung and blood samples from M. tuberculosis-infected C3HeB/FeJ mice to systematically map the relationship between pulmonary and peripheral transcriptional responses. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that inflammatory immune pathways, including type I interferon (IFN) responses, were commonly enriched across both tissues. Among the upregulated differentially expressed genes, 134 genes were shared between the lungs and blood. These shared transcripts were strongly associated with type I IFN signaling and neutrophil/myeloid-driven inflammatory responses. Genes with human orthologs were then ranked by differential expression magnitude and expression abundance across the two tissues, and the 10 highest-ranked genes were selected as a Top10 signature. This Top10 signature showed discriminatory performance across multiple TB disease states in independent human TB blood RNA-seq cohorts, comparable to that obtained using previously reported blood transcriptional signatures. Collectively, these findings suggest that blood transcriptional signatures in this mouse model share features with pulmonary inflammatory programs, providing experimental insight into how peripheral blood responses reflect disease-associated lung pathology during progressive TB. [IMPORTANCE] Blood transcriptional biomarkers are being investigated for the diagnosis and risk prediction of tuberculosis (TB). However, the relationship between blood RNA signatures and transcriptional programs in infected lungs remains poorly understood. In this study, we identified a common inflammatory transcriptional program shared across the blood and lungs of Mycobacterium tuberculosis-infected C3HeB/FeJ mice, a susceptible in vivo model resembling the key pathological features of human TB. The shared upregulated genes primarily included inflammatory genes related to type I interferon and neutrophil-mediated inflammatory responses. A representative Top10 gene signature derived from this shared program showed discriminatory performance across multiple clinical TB disease states in human TB cohorts, comparable to that obtained using previously reported blood transcriptional signatures. These findings suggest that blood transcriptional signatures overlap with the immune and inflammatory programs occurring in infected lungs and potentially provide a framework for the discovery of biomarkers for TB disease classification.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: BK polyomavirus genotype differs between biological compartments in children undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplants.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: BK polyomavirus (BKV) infection is widespread, with seroprevalence around 80%-90%. During hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT), BKV reactivation can cause hemorrhagic cystitis, thrombotic microangiopathy, and occasionally nephropathy. These conditions can lead to life-threatening organ injury. BKV is a small double-stranded DNA virus whose genome comprises early and late protein-coding regions and a non-coding control region. BKV is highly diverse and can be categorized into different genotypes based on variability within the viral protein 1 region. Mutations within the BKV coding and non-coding regions have been shown to affect virulence and cell tropism. In this study, we evaluated BKV genomes from the urine and/or plasma from 20 pediatric HSCT recipients to detect differences in BKV genotypes over time or between compartments. BKV-positive plasma and urine samples were collected, BKV was isolated and amplified, and viral genomes were sequenced by next-generation sequencing. In a group of 10 patients ("Compartmentalization group"), distinct BKV genotypes were detected in urine versus plasma in six patients (60%) at 1-month post-HSCT. BKV sequences among patients with concordant genotypes differed across compartments, despite sharing the same genotype. We also identified differences in T-cell epitopes that suggest some degree of immune selection, with differences greater across compartments than over time.IMPORTANCEBK polyomavirus (BKV) infection and/or reactivation causes severe toxicity after hematopoietic stem cell transplant, including hemorrhagic cystitis and thrombotic microangiopathy. Infections are commonly urinary, but viremia in addition to cystitis occurs in a proportion of cases. BKV detection in the blood is associated with an increased risk of BKV-associated hemorrhagic cystitis. The role of viral diversity in virulence, pathogenesis, and prognosis is poorly understood and is needed to develop prophylactic and therapeutic strategies. Uncovering BKV diversity in vivo will provide insight into how immune selection determines inter-compartmental spread. Understanding the role of BKV diversity throughout the body is important for therapeutic success, including virus-specific T-cell therapy and vaccine development.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Valnemulin, a repurposed oral drug, demonstrates dual activity against Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] The most prevalent bacterial sexually transmitted infections are caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. According to the World Health Organization, over 211 million cases were reported in 2020. Currently, ceftriaxone is the only recommended single-dose intramuscular therapy for gonorrhea, but it exhibits minimal to no efficacy against chlamydial infections. Azithromycin and doxycycline are recommended to treat C. trachomatis infections; however, N. gonorrhoeae has developed resistance to both. Hence, no single drug is available that can effectively target both pathogens. Through a drug repurposing approach, with a particular focus on uncommon or underexplored drugs, we identified valnemulin, a pleuromutilin derivative and veterinary antibiotic, as a potent dual-acting agent. Valnemulin showed potent activity against multidrug-resistant N. gonorrhoeae, with its minimum inhibitory concentrations as low as 0.03 μg/mL and retained activity against azithromycin-resistant N. gonorrhoeae. Additionally, valnemulin demonstrated anti-C. trachomatis activity at concentrations of 0.008 μg/mL. Moreover, valnemulin exhibited rapid bactericidal activity, a prolonged post-antibiotic effect, and a low propensity for resistance development. Insights into the mechanisms of action and binding sites were investigated as well. Valnemulin exhibited potent inhibition in the bacterial transcription/translation assay with an IC50 value of 0.07 μg/mL. Molecular docking with the 23S rRNA crystal structure revealed a highly favorable interaction with a binding affinity of -9.197 kcal mol-1. In a murine genital tract N. gonorrhoeae infection model, a single day of valnemulin treatment reduced gonococcal burden by 83%. Overall, our findings demonstrate that valnemulin is a promising candidate to treat sexually transmitted infections and deserves further investigation. [IMPORTANCE] The traditional drug discovery process is both time-consuming and costly, typically requiring 10-15 years and costing around $2 billion. Therefore, a therapeutic repurposing approach has emerged as an efficient alternative strategy for drug discovery that significantly reduces development time and cost. In an effort to identify new therapeutics against Chlamydia trachomatis/Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections through a drug repurposing approach, valnemulin was identified as a promising anti-C. trachomatis and anti-N. gonorrhoeae agent.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Plasmid-borne ThyA2 and DfrA mediate antimetabolite resistance in Staphylococcus aureus USA200.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Clinically used antimetabolites can impose selective pressures on bacteria, yet naturally occurring genetic determinants that shape bacterial responses to these compounds remain incompletely defined. Screening of methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and methicillin-resistant S. aureus strains identified a USA200 isolate with markedly reduced susceptibility to 5-fluorouracil (5FU), whereas most isolates were highly susceptible. We therefore investigated the genetic basis of 5FU resistance in this isolate. The elevated 5FU resistance was independent of PBP2a-mediated β-lactam resistance. Long-read sequencing revealed that USA200 carries a 36.92-kb plasmid encoding a divergent thymidylate synthase paralog, ThyA2, in addition to chromosomal ThyA. Heterologous expression of thyA2 increased 5FU resistance in susceptible S. aureus backgrounds, whereas deletion of thyA2 in USA200 reduced the 5FU minimum inhibitory concentration to susceptible-strain levels without altering cefuroxime or cefazolin susceptibility. The same plasmid also encoded an adjacent dfrA gene, and dfrA deletion markedly reduced trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole resistance without affecting 5FU or cephalosporin susceptibility. Thus, USA200 carries adjacent plasmid-borne determinants with separable antimetabolite-specific functions. ThyA2 mediates resistance to a chemotherapeutic pyrimidine analog, whereas DfrA mediates resistance to an antibacterial antifolate. These findings highlight the need to account for strain-specific resistance determinants when evaluating the antibacterial activity of 5FU.IMPORTANCECertain drugs used in cancer chemotherapy, such as 5-fluorouracil, can also inhibit bacterial growth, raising interest in their potential repurposing as antibacterial agents. However, whether bacteria already carry genes that counteract these effects is not well understood. We show that a clinical strain of the pathogen Staphylococcus aureus harbors a small plasmid encoding two physically linked but functionally independent genes: one that enables the bacterium to tolerate a chemotherapy drug, and another that enables resistance to an antibiotic combination used to treat staph infections. Neither gene affects the other drug's activity. These findings highlight that mobile genetic elements in bacteria can carry genes that influence susceptibility to non-antibiotic clinical drugs, with implications for antibacterial drug repurposing strategies and for understanding strain-specific responses to these drugs.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Transposon insertion sequencing identifies genetic determinants of intrinsic rifamycin resistance in Mycobacterium abscessus.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Mycobacterium abscessus exhibits intrinsic resistance to many antimicrobial agents, including rifampicin, a frontline anti-tuberculosis drug, severely limiting treatment options. Here, we used transposon insertion sequencing (Tn-Seq) to perform a genome-wide screen to identify genes required for intrinsic rifampicin resistance in M. abscessus. We uncovered candidate genes that confer intrinsic resistance to the rifamycin-class antibiotics, rifampicin, and rifabutin. The genes we identified included previously reported genes, such as arr, helR, and MAB_2807. By comparing our results with the rifampicin intrinsic resistance gene in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, we found that the mechanisms underlying rifampicin intrinsic resistance were distinct between the two species. The contribution of seven representative candidate genes to rifampicin resistance was confirmed by characterizing targeted gene deletion or transposon insertion mutants. Among these determinants, MAB_2807 was identified as a major efflux-based contributor to rifamycin resistance, and its disruption increased intracellular rifampicin accumulation. In addition to known resistance determinants, Tn-Seq revealed contributions from many genes involved in cell envelope processes to rifamycin resistance. Guided by this genetic signature, we evaluated the combined effects of cell wall-targeting antimicrobial agents with rifamycins. We found that rifamycins displayed selective synergistic interactions with specific β-lactam antimicrobial agents. Interestingly, rifamycin exposure altered cell envelope ultrastructure and increased accumulation of the peptidoglycan precursor UDP-N-acetylglucosamine, suggesting that rifampicin perturbs envelope-associated metabolic homeostasis. These findings highlight rifamycin-induced vulnerable cellular processes that may inform rational combination strategies. [IMPORTANCE] Rifamycins are cornerstone antibiotics for the treatment of mycobacterial infections, yet they are ineffective against Mycobacterium abscessus. Here, we used transposon insertion sequencing to systematically identify genes that contribute to intrinsic rifamycin resistance in M. abscessus. Because recent studies have shown that chemical modification of rifamycins can overcome specific intrinsic resistance mechanisms, a comprehensive understanding of these determinants could facilitate the development of next-generation rifamycins with improved activity against M. abscessus. In addition, we unexpectedly found that rifamycin exposure alters cell envelope structure, the intracellular levels of a key metabolic intermediate in peptidoglycan biosynthesis, and susceptibility to certain β-lactams in M. abscessus. These findings may help guide the rational development of combination therapeutic strategies with rifamycins.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: A two-step model of FtsZ-ring disassembly in Bacillus subtilis.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: Bacillus subtilis grows and divides by binary fission directed by medial localization of cell division protein FtsZ. Disruption of either the Min system or EzrA results in aberrant FtsZ positioning. Here, we grow cells in microfluidic channels and find that cells lacking MinD or EzrA appear to be similarly defective in Z-ring disassembly after septation, but play different roles as simultaneous disruption results in a synergistic defect in division. Moreover, we account for a low frequency of minicell formation in the absence of EzrA, as MinD but not EzrA is necessary for removal of ZapA from polar Z-rings. Finally, overexpression of MinCD inhibits division through pervasive Z-ring disassembly, but appears to concentrate ZapA through localized sequestration. Combined, our results indicate a closer relationship between MinCD and ZapA than previously recognized and show that Z-ring disassembly can be genetically separated into discrete steps. We propose a two-step model for Z-ring disassembly that mirrors the assembly process, such that after and/or during septation, the Z-ring separately decondenses, and protofilaments are disassembled to monomers for recycling.IMPORTANCEBacteria divide by polymerizing and condensing the cell division protein FtsZ and encode a suite of proteins that control FtsZ spatial localization. Here, we compare two FtsZ regulatory proteins, MinD and EzrA, in the bacterium Bacillus subtilis and find that they are required for the disassembly of FtsZ at two different steps after division. Based on our results, we propose a two-step model of Z-ring disassembly where FtsZ protofilaments are decondensed and depolymerized separately. Finally, most regulators of FtsZ tend to be considered from the standpoint of Z-ring assembly, and we assert that Z-ring disassembly and monomer recycling are just as important for timely division.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: A NanAKE-like pathway enables sialic acid catabolism in gut microbiome member Hungatella hathewayi.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Sialic acids are abundant components of host- and diet-derived glycans in the human gut that shape microbial fitness and interspecies competition. Free sialic acids can be a nutrient source but also stimulate inflammation and pathogen colonization. Escherichia coli and Bacteroides spp. catabolize sialic acids via the NanAKE and NanLE-RokA pathways, yet the metabolic capacity of many microbiome members remains undefined. To identify sialic acid-catabolizing bacteria, we cultured fecal samples from healthy human donors. The gut anaerobe Hungatella hathewayi was selected under sialic acid-supplemented conditions. H. hathewayi is a poorly characterized gram-positive Lachnospiraceae species associated with long-lived individuals and purine metabolism. Here we establish that H. hathewayi grows robustly on sialic acids as a sole carbon source. H. hathewayi encodes a NanAKE-like pathway in a locus containing a nanA ortholog divergently oriented to nanKE orthologs. We functionally validated these orthologs through growth assays and heterologous complementation in E. coli knockout strains. Comparative analyses further showed that key catalytic residues in H. hathewayi NanA are conserved despite overall sequence divergence from E. coli. H. hathewayi also encodes putative transport and regulatory proteins near the nan-like genes. These putative proteins are not orthologous to the E. coli NanT transporter or NanR regulator but are instead related to transporters and regulators identified in other gut anaerobes. Together, these findings identify H. hathewayi as an overlooked but capable sialic acid degrader and expand our understanding of sialic acid metabolism within the human gut microbiome. [IMPORTANCE] Sialic acids play an important role in mammalian and microbial signaling. Excess free sialic acids increase susceptibility to gut pathogens and induce inflammation. Gut bacteria can consume free sialic acids, and the catabolic pathways involved are conserved across diverse bacteria, including Escherichia coli and Bacteroides fragilis. We identify Hungatella hathewayi as another bacterium capable of sialic acid consumption and define the enzymes responsible. H. hathewayi is a prevalent member of the human gut microbiome that is enriched in the gut microbiomes of long-lived individuals and is expected to contribute to purine degradation to limit gout risk. Defining sialic acid catabolism in non-model species will elucidate the evolution and conservation of this pathway as well as microbiome sialic acid metabolism.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: AlgR regulates expression of the biofilm adhesin CdrA in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] The opportunistic pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa forms antibiotic-tolerant biofilms that cause persistent and chronic infections. Knowledge of the mechanistic basis of biofilm formation is needed for future development of medicine against tenacious biofilm infections. Here, we demonstrate that the transcriptional regulator AlgR is essential for expression of the cdrA gene, which encodes a biofilm adhesin. Using transcriptional reporters and protein analysis, we show that deletion of algR abolishes cdrA transcription and production of the CdrA protein. Electrophoretic mobility shift assays provided evidence that AlgR binds directly to the cdrA promoter. Phenotypic analysis showed that algR mutants are defective in CdrA-mediated cell aggregation. Disruption of a putative AlgR binding box eliminated binding of AlgR to the cdrA promoter and abolished CdrA-dependent aggregation. Epistasis analysis indicated that AlgR is epistatic to FleQ in the regulation of cdrA. Experiments with fimS, stk1, and algR-D54N mutants suggested that induction of cdrA occurs without phosphorylation of AlgR. [IMPORTANCE] Our findings establish AlgR as a direct transcriptional activator of cdrA and highlight the protein as a central regulator of biofilm-associated traits in P. aeruginosa and a potential target for strategies aimed at controlling biofilm-related infections.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Effects of increased 2',3'-cNMPs in E. coli: pleiotropic transcriptional changes and direct regulation of a nucleotide metabolic enzyme.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] 2',3'-Cyclic nucleotide monophosphates (2',3'-cNMPs) are ubiquitous intracellular small molecules with similarities to known nucleotide second messengers. This work investigated the effects of increased intracellular 2',3'-cNMP levels on the Escherichia coli transcriptome across several growth phases and two experimental methods. Results of the analysis highlighted dramatic changes in the transcriptome as cells enter stationary phase, including altered amino acid metabolism and metal homeostasis. Phenotypic studies validated the transcriptional changes and identified a role for 2',3'-cNMPs in modulating stationary-phase cell density, as well as investigated possible mechanisms of 2',3'-cAMP-mediated regulation. This work provides insights into the physiological effects of 2',3'-cNMP signaling and highlights how modulating 2',3'-cNMP levels could potentially be used to control bacterial behavior. [IMPORTANCE] Bacteria utilize a range of intracellular signaling molecules, including nucleotide second messengers, to alter behavior in response to environmental stimuli and growth phase. Understanding the roles of poorly understood signaling molecules will provide new insights into how intracellular pathways are controlled and improve predictive models of bacterial behavior. This study demonstrates that in Escherichia coli, increased 2',3'-cyclic nucleotide monophosphate levels modulate the transcriptome, particularly during the transition to stationary phase when concentrations naturally decrease. Effects of maintaining 2',3'-cAMP levels as cells exit the exponential phase include altered metal resistance and activity of adenylosuccinate synthase, which affects nucleotide pools, highlighting roles in important bacterial phenotypes.

Journal of Bacteriology.title: Identifying phage host receptors using TraDIS.
Journal of Bacteriology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] The growing antimicrobial resistance crisis has sparked renewed interest in using bacteriophage (phage) as a treatment for antibiotic-resistant infections. Phage are viruses that infect and often kill bacteria and have served as key models for many molecular biology studies. There are many complex phage-bacterial interactions that dictate the success or failure of the phage life cycle, but many of these are not well understood or characterized. These include the specific interactions to recognize a bacterium during the infection process, bacterial phage defense mechanisms, and metabolic pathways that are key to phage replication. In this study, a novel Escherichia coli phage, Arnold, is characterized, and the genome sequence is reported. We then use transposon-directed insertion-site sequencing to screen a library of E. coli mutants to identify over 200 genes involved in Arnold phage infection or in phage resistance. Using this approach, we identified both an outer membrane protein (BtuB, vitamin B12 transporter) and an inner membrane protein (SdaC, serine/proton symporter) that are essential for phage infection; deletions in these genes were shown to provide immunity to infection by this phage. Understanding the genetic basis of phage infection and phage resistance should allow us to select or design phage to target specific bacterial pathogens in the future. [IMPORTANCE] Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global threat to modern health, and new solutions are needed to fight multi-drug resistant infections. One promising solution are bacteriophages, viruses that naturally infect and kill bacteria. Phage infection is very strain specific, governed by the interaction of phage proteins with a cell surface receptor. In order to understand the rules that govern which phage can infect which bacteria, we need to identify these interacting partners. We report the genome of a phage infecting Escherichia coli and use transposon insertion sequencing to identify genes involved in phage infection, including what we propose are the cell surface receptors required for infection. This knowledge is essential for understanding and potentially engineering targeted phage treatments against specific bacterial pathogens.

eLife.title: ATP8B1–TMEM30B flippase activity maintains stereocilia lipid asymmetry required for hearing
eLife.abstract: Sensory hair cells convert sound-induced vibrations into electrical signals through a process called mechano-electrical transduction (MET). While the protein components of the MET complex are well studied, increasing evidence indicates that MET channel properties are significantly modulated by the surrounding lipid bilayer. The asymmetric distribution of membrane lipids between the inner and outer membrane leaflets is well established to shape membrane mechanics. The recent discovery that the core MET components TMC1 and TMC2 also act as lipid scramblases suggests a direct role for membrane lipid asymmetry in the dynamic shaping of auditory transduction. Because scramblase activity of TMC1/2 disrupts lipid asymmetry, we hypothesized that an opposing flippase may be required to restore and maintain lipid asymmetry. Here, we identify the P4-ATPase ATP8B1 and its chaperone TMEM30B as selectively expressed in mouse outer hair cells (OHCs), enriched in stereocilia, and upregulated following the onset of MET and hearing. Loss of either protein results in elevated auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds, phosphatidylserine (PS) externalization, and rapid hair-cell degeneration, demonstrating that lipid homeostasis is crucial for OHC survival. Together, these findings establish ATP8B1 and TMEM30B as key regulators of membrane lipid asymmetry in sensory hair cells and establish TMEM30B as a novel deafness gene.

eLife.title: Pre-rRNA represses gene transcription in the XY body of male germ cells
eLife.abstract: Nucleolus is disassembled when the nuclear envelope breaks down during mitosis prophase. However, the dynamics of nucleolus in meiotic prophase remain unclear. Here, by tracking nucleolar components of spermatocytes in mice, we show that the nucleolus is fragmented even before the breakdown of the nuclear envelope. Instead of dissolving in nucleoplasm or cytoplasm, the nucleolar components are reaggregated and fused with the XY body during prophase I of meiosis. The dynamic relocation of the nucleolar components to the XY body is governed by the ATR-dependent signaling pathway. Moreover, the relocated pre-ribosomal RNA (pre-rRNA) covers the entire X and Y chromosomes. The treatment with RNA polymerase I inhibitor BMH-21 only disrupts the accumulation of pre-rRNA but not other nucleolar components on the X and Y chromosomes. Surprisingly, this disruption of pre-rRNA induces the recruitment of RNA polymerase II to the XY body and partially abolishes meiotic sex chromosome inactivation (MSCI). Taken together, this study reveals pre-rRNA as a key epigenetic regulator for MSCI.

eLife.title: SATAY-based chemogenomic screening uncovers antifungal resistance mechanisms and key determinants of ATI-2307 and chitosan sensitivity
eLife.abstract: Multidrug-resistant fungal pathogens are a serious threat to public health and global food security. Mitigation requires the discovery of antifungal compounds with novel modes of action along with a comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms governing antifungal resistance. Here, we apply saturated transposon analysis in yeast (SATAY), a powerful transposon sequencing method in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, to uncover loss- and gain-of-function mutations conferring resistance to 20 different antifungal compounds. These screens identify a diverse array of novel resistance mechanisms and multiple modes of action. SATAY is performed in drug-sensitive strains to generate chemogenomic profiles for compounds that lack activity against conventional laboratory strains. This study therefore provides a significant resource for exploring cellular responses to chemical stresses. We discover that the natural antifungal chitosan electrostatically interacts with cell wall mannosylphosphate and that the transporter Hol1 concentrates the novel antifungal ATI-2307 within yeast. This latter finding presents an avenue for drug design initiatives but also unveils a straightforward evolutionary path to ATI-2307 resistance with minimal fitness cost.

eLife.title: A step towards modelling amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in primates
eLife.abstract: A new primate model offers a promising first step towards reproducing the spread of ALS pathology across synapses, although important differences from the stereotyped patterns observed in human disease remain to be addressed.

Genome Research.title: Chromosome-scale genome assembly and annotation of Octodon degus.
Genome Research.abstract: High-quality reference genomes are essential for comparative and functional genomics yet remain unavailable for many emerging model organisms. Here, we report OctDeg2.0, a chromosome-scale genome assembly and annotation of the degu (Octodon degus), generated using Pacific Biosciences (PacBio) HiFi long-read sequencing and Hi-C scaffolding from a single male individual. Octodon degus is of growing interest as a natural animal model for aging and Alzheimer's disease research. The 3.4 billion bp assembly comprises 28 autosomes and both X and Y Chromosomes with markedly improved contiguity and completeness over the prior assembly while maintaining high base accuracy. The new assembly provides substantially enhanced gene annotation, clearer resolution of chromatin architecture and cis-regulatory element landscapes, and much improved characterization of repetitive features, including centromere-associated and segmentally duplicated regions. We present a streamlined and reproducible pipeline for high-resolution de novo genome assembly and gene annotation applicable to other emerging model organisms. This work establishes a robust genomic resource for studying molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying degu biology.

Genome Research.title: Developmental transcriptomic analysis of cultured primary mouse cortical neurons reveals sex-specific expression of neuropeptides.
Genome Research.abstract: Primary neuronal cultures derived from mouse tissue serve as an essential model for investigating neuronal development and function. Despite this, comprehensive developmental and sex-specific transcriptomic profiles in primary neurons have not been defined. Here, we perform multiplexed RNA sequencing of neurons derived from male and female cortices across time. We validate this approach by assessing established neuronal maturation genes and identify highly stable genes to serve as controls across development. Next, using linear modeling and temporal regression, we define developmentally regulated transcripts, longitudinal expression dynamics, and gene signatures associated with transition states throughout development. Unexpectedly, this also reveals sex-specific effects on autosomal genes that emerge only after neuronal maturation even in the absence of in vivo cues. Most notably, neuropeptide genes Cortistatin and Neurokinin A are more highly expressed in female neurons. Furthermore, exposure to these neuropeptides elicits distinct transcriptional responses in male- versus female-derived cultures. These findings provide a valuable resource and reveal sex-specific autosomal transcriptional signatures that emerge in neurons maintained ex vivo.

Genome Research.title: A new noninvasive prenatal paternity test based on double-nucleotide polymorphisms abates sequencing uncertainties and improves sensitivity.
Genome Research.abstract: Noninvasive prenatal paternity testing (NIPAT) based on fetal cell-free DNA (fetal cfDNA) has gained increasing relevance in forensic genetics. However, its applicability and reliability are often limited by the low fetal DNA fraction and by high-throughput sequencing errors that can be misinterpreted as inherited paternal variants. Here, we present NEWPAT, a novel NIPAT approach based on double-nucleotide polymorphisms (DNPs), namely, biallelic variants composed of two adjacent nucleotides arising from a single mutational event. These markers offer a key advantage compared to single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs): The likelihood of both positions being affected by independent sequencing errors is extremely low, thus improving the specificity of fetal DNA detection. We develop a targeted amplicon-based panel including 979 markers (845 autosomal and 80 X Chromosome DNPs, plus 54 Y SNPs) and test at depths ranging from 1000× to 10,000× on 42 individuals, including genomic DNA from four families, two artificial maternal-child mixtures simulating cfDNA, and actual cfDNA from 12 pregnant women plus the putative biological fathers. We observe a DNP sequencing error rate of 8.9 × 10-5, namely, about 12 times lower than the observed single-base error rate. By exploiting the full range of sequencing depths at loci supporting the fetal genotype, we obtain combined paternity index curves that consistently lead to the correct paternity attribution or exclusion in all true or false mother-father pairs. Notably, NEWPAT proves effective even at fetal cfDNA levels as low as 0.2%, when existing SNP-based protocols lead to inconclusive results, offering a highly sensitive and accurate NIPAT strategy.

Genome Research.title: Interindividual gene expression variability implies stable regulation of brain-biased genes across organs in three ray-finned fishes.
Genome Research.abstract: Phenotypic variation among individuals provides the raw material for evolution, and gene expression is a key mediator between genetic and phenotypic variation. As for phenotypes, the range of gene expression is limited and biased by evolutionary and developmental constraints. Observed expression variability because of biomolecular stochasticity and cell-to-cell heterogeneity has been well studied in isogenic populations of unicellular organisms. However, for multicellular organisms with a diversity of cells and tissues sharing the same genetic background, the interplay between expression variability, gene and organ function, and gene regulation remains an open question. Here, we use highly multiplexed 3'-end bulk RNA sequencing to generate transcriptome profiles spanning at least nine organs in outbred individuals of three ray-finned fish species: zebrafish, Northern pike, and spotted gar. Per organ, we quantify individual-to-individual gene expression variability independent of mean expression level. Lowly variable genes are enriched in cellular housekeeping functions, whereas highly variable genes are enriched in stimulus-response functions. Furthermore, highly variable genes evolve under weaker purifying selection at the protein-coding sequence, indicating that intraspecies expression variability predicts interspecies protein sequence divergence. Genes that are broadly expressed across organs are both highly expressed and lowly variable, whereas organ-biased genes are typically highly variable within their top organ. Among organ-biased genes, patterns of expression variance are dependent on the top organ. Specifically, brain- and gonad-biased genes have lowly variable expression across different organs, suggesting stabilizing selection. These patterns suggest that gene regulatory mechanisms evolve under organ-specific selective pressures.

Genome Research.title: Refining indel-trait and structural variant-trait associations with LAVrefiner.
Genome Research.abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are major sources of human genetic diversity. Despite advances in SV discovery, most single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-centric frameworks overlook sequence-level information and encode overlapping variants as independent features, potentially reducing power in association studies, biasing heritability estimation, and limiting prediction accuracy. Here, we present LAVrefiner, a scalable, sequence-aware method that decomposes overlapping sequence-resolved SVs and indels into nonoverlapping refined sequence components and generates genotype matrices compatible with standard SNP-based analyses. In tandem repeat (TR) regions, LAVrefiner further supports motif-aware allele comparison and repeat copy-number estimation. When applied to variants from The 1000 Genomes Project, LAVrefiner identifies 224,708 refined variants. Simulations show that LAVrefiner is fast and memory-efficient while maintaining robust genotype representations under TR-associated sequencing noise. In gene expression analyses, models combining LAVrefiner-derived copy-number estimates with refined variants yield the highest heritability estimates and prediction accuracy in short tandem repeat (STR) and variable-number tandem repeat (VNTR) regions, outperforming models based on the original SV/indel representation and existing TR copy-number tools. Cis-expression quantitative trait locus (cis-eQTL) mapping further shows that refined variants can localize regulatory signals to specific sequence components, including an independent VNTR-derived signal at the TFRC locus. Together, LAVrefiner provides an efficient, context-aware strategy for integrating sequence-resolved SVs and indels into existing genetic analysis frameworks.

Genome Research.title: Conditional diffusion for single-cell Hi-C data imputation and enhancement with scHiC-Diff.
Genome Research.abstract: Single-cell high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (scHi-C) enables the analysis of cell-to-cell variability in three-dimensional (3D) genome organization, but its utility is severely limited by pervasive technical dropouts, leading to extremely sparse contact maps. Accurately identifying dropout events and imputing the corresponding missing chromatin contacts remains a challenging problem, as technical dropouts are confounded with genuine absences of chromatin interactions. Existing imputation and enhancement methods often rely on smoothing strategies or restrictive parametric likelihood assumptions, which may obscure fine-scale chromatin structures and cell-specific features. Here, we present scHiC-Diff, a conditional diffusion-based framework for scHi-C data imputation and enhancement. scHiC-Diff employs a forward process that progressively perturbs contact maps and a reverse denoising process that reconstructs chromatin interactions from noisy observations. To better capture long-range dependencies in complex 3D genome structures, scHi-C contact matrices are treated as masked images and modeled using a Diffusion Transformer (DiT). Across two complementary simulated data sets and three real scHi-C data sets, scHiC-Diff improves the recovery of chromatin interaction patterns and enhances downstream analyses compared with existing methods. Application to a developmental scHi-C data set further demonstrates improved reconstruction of chromatin organization and enhanced chromatin loop detection.

Molecular Biology and Evolution.title: Reimagining inflammatory bowel disease in the age of artificial intelligence: discovery, care, education, and sustainability for the next decade
Molecular Biology and Evolution.abstract: AbstractArtificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly evolving from task-specific algorithms to multimodal foundation models capable of integrating heterogeneous biological and clinical data across the health-care continuum. In inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), this transformation offers an unprecedented opportunity to move beyond fragmented analyses toward a unified understanding and management of disease. Artificial intelligence is emerging as the connective infrastructure linking scientific discovery, therapeutic development, patient care, education, and health-care delivery systems into continuously learning ecosystems. In this viewpoint, we explore how AI may reshape IBD over the next decade through 5 interconnected domains. Advances in multimodal AI accelerate biological discovery by integrating multiomics, spatial biology, and foundation models to identify mechanistic disease endotypes. Simultaneously, AI can shorten the path from molecular discovery to therapeutic innovation by supporting target identification, predicting protein structure, drug positioning, and adaptive clinical trial design. These scientific advances converge at the bedside, where multimodal AI may transform patient care from reactive management to predictive precision medicine through integrated diagnostics, digital biomarkers, real-time monitoring and individualized risk prediction. Beyond clinical care, AI is redefining medical education by enabling adaptive learning, explainable decision support, and democratized specialist expertise, while contributing to sustainable health care through optimized resource allocation, workforce support, and continuously learning systems. Realizing this vision will require robust governance, interoperability, prospective validation, and equitable implementation. If responsibly deployed, AI holds the potential to redefine IBD diagnosis, classification, therapeutic strategies and management within an intelligent ecosystem able to accelerate discovery, personalize care, and improve outcomes for patients and health-care systems alike.

PLOS Biology.title: When should adaptation arise from a polygenic response versus few large-effect changes?
PLOS Biology.abstract: by William R. Milligan, Laura K. Hayward, Guy Sella When will adaptation involve a few genetic changes of large effect versus a polygenic response? There are compelling reasons to expect polygenic adaptation to be common, yet direct evidence is lacking. Conversely, there are hundreds of examples of large-effect adaptations across species, but it is unclear whether they occur frequently within any given species. These different lines of evidence are hard to synthesize, in part due to the lack of theory that relates them. To address this gap, we frame the question in terms of the properties of an adaptive trait. We ask how the genetic basis of adaptation depends on key aspects of genetic variation in the trait and on the degree to which its selection pressures have changed. To this end, we consider a quantitative trait subject to stabilizing selection and model its response when a population at mutation–selection–drift balance experiences a sudden shift in the trait optimum. Using this model, we delimit how the contributions of large-effect and polygenic changes to adaptation depend on the genetics and ecology of adaptive traits, as well as on other salient factors. Thus, we formulate testable predictions for when different modes of adaptation are expected.

mBio.title: The mechanosensitive channel MscS links lipoteichoic acid synthesis alterations to beta-lactam sensitivity in Staphylococcus aureus.
mBio.abstract: Lipoteichoic acid (LTA) is an essential cell envelope polymer in Staphylococcus aureus and contributes to beta-lactam resistance in methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA). Mutations that alter LTA synthesis sensitize MRSA to beta-lactam antibiotics, but the mechanism connecting the envelope polymer defects to antibiotic susceptibility has remained unclear. Here, using suppressor mutants with a mutation in RNA polymerase subunits, we found that LTA synthesis defects increased expression of a ParB-like protein and the mechanosensitive channel MscS. This locus was repressed in RNA polymerase suppressor mutants, which restored beta-lactam resistance, whereas induced expression of both genes reduced resistance. Increased ParBL-MscS expression was associated with decreased intracellular potassium and reduced cyclic di-AMP (c-di-AMP), linking altered membrane-envelope physiology to second messenger signaling. LTA synthesis mutants also showed reduced production of penicillin-binding protein 4 (PBP4), an important determinant of beta-lactam resistance. Modest restoration of PBP4 improved resistance in the mutant with reduced LTA abundance, whereas the mutant producing elongated LTA showed a distinct response, indicating that different LTA defects impose different envelope stresses. Also, under reduced LTA conditions, increased c-di-AMP level alone was not sufficient to restore PBP4 expression and beta-lactam resistance. Together, these findings identify a potassium-dependent pathway connecting LTA synthesis, mechanosensitive channel activity, c-di-AMP signaling, PBP4 production, and beta-lactam resistance. This work reveals how cell envelope perturbations are converted into cytoplasmic regulatory responses that control antibiotic susceptibility and suggests that ion homeostasis and c-di-AMP signaling may be exploitable pathways for restoring beta-lactam efficacy against MRSA.IMPORTANCEAntibiotic-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), is difficult to treat because it can withstand many beta-lactam antibiotics. Changes in lipoteichoic acid (LTA), a major cell-envelope polymer, increase beta-lactam sensitivity, but the underlying mechanism has been unclear. Here, we show that LTA synthesis defects activate a pathway involving the predicted membrane channel MscS. This pathway lowers intracellular potassium, reduces cyclic di-AMP signaling, and decreases production of PBP4, a cell-wall synthesis enzyme that contributes to beta-lactam resistance. These changes make MRSA more vulnerable to beta-lactam antibiotics. Our findings show that antibiotic resistance depends not only on drug targets but also on coordination between the cell envelope, ion homeostasis, and intracellular signaling. This connection identifies physiological pathways that may be exploited to restore beta-lactam efficacy against resistant S. aureus.
